University capstone projects require students to work with information from multiple sources, including general capstone guidance, project briefs, proposals, sponsor requirements, meeting outcomes, milestones, and other project documentation. As projects progress, this information can become distributed across different documents and communication channels, making it difficult for students and other project stakeholders to quickly locate and interpret information relevant to a particular project activity.
The broader opportunity is an AI-assisted capstone project management system that could progressively support capstone project activities through AI-assisted access to project information and project-management functionality. However, developing the entire system is outside the boundaries of this current project. The project, therefore, focuses on a specific Micro-SaaS module: an AI-assisted Capstone Project Assistant.
The Capstone Assistant will provide a central conversational interface through which authorized users can interact with both general capstone information and contextual information belonging to specific projects.

General capstone assistance, using approved general capstone information.
Project-specific assistance, using information associated with an authorized capstone project, including project documents, meetings, milestones, and basic project information.
Trellis Data's sovereign Agentaus AI will be used for natural-language response generation.
As the project involves the practical integration of a Large Language Model (LLM), the prototype will also address key applied-AI considerations identified in the sponsor brief, including prompt design and refinement, hallucination mitigation, data privacy, and evaluation of AI response accuracy, latency, and usability. These considerations will be incorporated into the design, testing, and monitoring of the prototype.
The Micro-SaaS is intended to reduce the effort required to locate, interpret, and use relevant capstone and project information. The current project therefore focuses specifically on information access and contextual AI assistance, rather than attempting to implement the entire future AI-assisted capstone project management system.

Capstone projects allow students to integrate knowledge and skills developed throughout their studies while working on complex and often industry-oriented problems. However, the nature of these projects can create challenges in organising project information, monitoring progress, maintaining documentation, communicating with supervisors, and locating relevant guidance throughout the project lifecycle. Previous research has consequently explored digital platforms and project-management tools to provide students and academic staff with more structured support during Capstone projects.
One of the earlier approaches was WIER (Web Industrial Experience Resource), evaluated by Ceddia and Sheard (2002) with 175 final-year IT students. WIER supported several stakeholders, including students, clients, supervisors and coordinators, and provided project-management facilities, reusable artefacts from previous projects and administrative support. The evaluation indicated that students generally considered the system a useful resource. An important motivation behind WIER was to make knowledge and resources from previous projects available to future students, reducing the need for students to repeatedly address problems already encountered by earlier groups. This research established the value of centralising Capstone resources and project information, although users still needed to locate and interpret relevant resources through a conventional web-based environment.
Olarte et al. (2014) further investigated digital support for Capstone projects through a web-based management tool for Computer Science Engineering students and advisors.

Olarte et al. (2014) further investigated digital support for Capstone projects through a web-based management tool for Computer Science Engineering students and advisors. Their research identified issues including project delays, unstructured development processes, poor-quality outcomes and student isolation during long-term Capstone work. The developed system addressed these issues through planning and monitoring, project profiles, deliverable management, meeting minutes, visibility of peer progress and communication between students and advisors working on similar projects. The system also demonstrated the value of maintaining project records, as meeting minutes and progress information could subsequently assist students when preparing their final reports. This work highlights the benefits of centralising project information and supervision activities; however, interaction with this information remained primarily through conventional application interfaces rather than conversational access to project knowledge.
The value of digital project-management support in collaborative Capstone environments was also investigated by Wahyudin, Lestari and Haritman (2024). Their study used a project-management application to support collaborative project-based learning, incorporating functions such as scheduling, communication, notifications and project monitoring. The authors reported generally positive findings regarding student motivation, engagement and collaboration and concluded that project-management applications can facilitate collaboration, monitoring and planning within student projects.

Recent research demonstrates a shift towards incorporating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Capstone and higher-education project environments. Albalawi (2026) presented the Smart Innovation Hub, an AI-enabled educational innovation platform supporting challenge-based projects and multidisciplinary coordination. The platform integrates challenge intake, participant profiling, AI-supported recommendations, interdisciplinary team formation, mentor alignment, milestone tracking, workflow governance and human-in-the-loop review. Its AI framework combines semantic similarity with structured constraints to support matching between challenges, students, mentors and institutional resources. The platform also incorporates role-based access controls, institutional permissions and human oversight, demonstrating the importance of governance when AI is applied within educational environments.

Although this demonstrates substantial use of AI within Capstone-related processes, its AI functionality is principally concerned with recommendation, matching and institutional coordination rather than conversational retrieval of information from an individual project's artefacts.
Alongside Capstone-specific systems, advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provide an important technical foundation for conversational educational assistance. Li et al. (2025) systematically reviewed RAG applications in education and identified limitations of conventional LLMs, particularly hallucination and reliance on static internal knowledge. RAG supplements an LLM by retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge source and incorporating that information into the generation process. This can improve factual accuracy and enable responses to use more current and contextually relevant knowledge. Their review covers applications including educational question-answering systems, chatbots and tutoring systems, demonstrating that retrieval-based approaches can ground educational responses in relevant source material. Importantly, the authors also highlight that RAG does not completely eliminate hallucination because the retrieved information itself may be incomplete, irrelevant or outdated.

Within the University of Canberra Capstone context, an existing initiative, QStop, also demonstrates the relevance of conversational AI. QStop is an AI Query Agent introduced as part of a pilot with the UC AI Steering Group to investigate whether AI-supported query assistance can provide students with quicker and accurate responses to frequently asked unit related questions. As an existing institutional initiative, QStop provides important practical context for the proposed research because it demonstrates that conversational AI is already being explored for general Capstone information and frequently asked questions. The proposed project builds on the broader research direction demonstrated by such educational AI initiatives by investigating conversational assistance that can also use authorised project-specific context, including project documents, meeting information and milestones.
Overall, the literature demonstrates an evolution from centralised Capstone resource repositories and project-management platforms towards AI-supported educational systems.

The chosen solution is a web-based AI-assisted Capstone Project Assistant developed as a focused Micro-SaaS prototype. The system will provide authorised Students, Mentors, the Convenor and Administrator with a conversational interface for accessing relevant Capstone information.
The assistant will support two main types of interaction:
General Capstone assistance
Project-specific assistance
Trellis Data's Agentaus AI will be used for natural-language response generation. Rather than allowing the AI to answer solely from general model knowledge, the application will retrieve relevant information and provide it as context to Agentaus. This approach is intended to improve response relevance and reduce unsupported or hallucinated information.
The prototype will also include configurable prompt templates, prompt version tracking, user feedback and AI performance monitoring so that the quality of the assistant can be evaluated and improved during development.

The selected approach was chosen because the main problem identified in the project is not the absence of project-management software, but the difficulty of quickly locating and interpreting relevant information distributed across Capstone guidance, project documents, meeting records, milestones and other project artefacts.
A conversational AI assistant provides users with a natural-language method of accessing this information without requiring them to manually search through multiple documents. The proposed solution is also suitable for the project's 10-week development period because it focuses on a specific Micro-SaaS module rather than attempting to develop the complete future Capstone project-management platform.
Another important reason for selecting this approach is the opportunity to investigate practical applied-AI challenges. The project can evaluate not only whether Agentaus generates a response, but whether the response is relevant, grounded in retrieved information, avoids unsupported claims and is returned within an acceptable response time.

Three retrieval approaches were considered for identifying relevant information before sending context to Agentaus:

Table row 2: Keyword Search | Simple and lightweight | Limited when users use different terminology
Table row 3: TF-IDF + Cosine Similarity | Lightweight, local, explainable and suitable for a controlled document collection | Less semantic than embedding-based retrieval
Table row 4: Vector Retrieval | Strong semantic matching and better future scalability | Requires additional embedding and vector-database infrastructure
TF-IDF with cosine similarity has been selected as the preferred retrieval method for the prototype. This method provides sufficient retrieval capability for a controlled collection of Capstone and project documents while remaining lightweight and explainable. It also avoids introducing vector-database and embedding infrastructure that may add unnecessary complexity within the 10-week project period.
Vector retrieval will remain a potential future enhancement if prototype evaluation demonstrates that TF-IDF retrieval is insufficient.

JSON, SQLite and PostgreSQL were considered for storing system information. SQLite has been selected as the preferred database for the prototype because it provides relational data storage while remaining lightweight and simple to deploy. Relational storage is useful for maintaining relationships between users, roles, projects, meetings, milestones and project access.
JSON alone would provide simpler initial development but is less suitable for managing relational user and project-access requirements. PostgreSQL would provide greater production scalability but introduces additional deployment complexity that is unnecessary for the current Micro-SaaS prototype.

A browser-based interface will be used because the system is intended to support multiple user roles and provide access without requiring desktop software installation. For the MVP, rapid development will be prioritised over advanced interface customisation. A lightweight web framework such as Streamlit may therefore be used where appropriate because it supports rapid development of AI-based prototypes and can provide the required conversational interface, project selection and administrative views within the available project timeframe.
A fully customised front-end and back-end architecture provides greater interface flexibility but requires significantly greater development effort. This may be considered for future development if the prototype is expanded into a production system.

Structured prompt templates will be developed separately for general Capstone assistance and project-specific assistance. For a general Capstone question, the application will retrieve relevant approved general Capstone information and provide that information to Agentaus as context. For a project-specific question, the application will first confirm that the user is authorised to access the selected project and will retrieve information only from that project.
Where appropriate, general and project-specific information may be combined.
The intended workflow is:
User Question
→ Identify User and Role
→ Determine General or Project Context
→ Check Project Authorisation
→ Retrieve Relevant Information
→ Construct Prompt
→ Agentaus AI
→ Generate Grounded Response
→ Record Performance Information and Feedback
If sufficient information cannot be retrieved, the assistant will provide appropriate fallback guidance rather than intentionally generating unsupported information.

A general-purpose chatbot without controlled retrieval was considered but was not selected because it would provide less control over the information used to answer Capstone questions and could increase the likelihood of generic or unsupported responses.
A complete Capstone project-management system was also considered. However, implementing task allocation, advanced scheduling, risk-management workflows, automated analytics and other comprehensive project-management functionality would significantly increase the project scope and would not be realistic within the current 10-week development period.
A vector-database-based retrieval architecture was considered but has been deferred because the additional embedding and vector infrastructure is not currently necessary for demonstrating the core concept.
The selected approach therefore provides an appropriate balance between functionality, technical complexity, AI experimentation and the available development timeframe.

The project will be delivered by a four-member student project team with guidance from the academic supervisor/mentor and input from the project sponsor where required. A lightweight governance structure will be used because the project has a limited 10-week delivery period.
The project team will be responsible for day-to-day planning, development, integration, testing and documentation. Responsibilities will be allocated across the four members based on project activities and technical requirements, while major scope and design decisions will be discussed collectively.

Quality assurance will be conducted throughout the development of the Capstone Assistant to ensure that the final prototype meets the agreed functional, non-functional and AI-quality requirements. Testing will be incorporated into the development iterations so that defects, integration issues and AI-response problems can be identified and addressed progressively. The project will use unit testing, integration and functional testing, access-control testing, AI response evaluation, and User Acceptance Testing (UAT). Relevant tests will also be repeated following significant changes to reduce the risk of regression issues.
Unit testing will verify individual system components and core system requirements, including role and project-access validation, information retrieval, meeting and milestone operations, fallback behaviour, and Agentaus API error handling.
Integration and functional testing will verify that the major system components operate correctly together and that the prototype satisfies its defined functional requirements. This will include testing the complete interaction flow from a user's question, through authorised information retrieval and Agentaus AI processing, to the generated response. Core functions such as authentication, project selection, document handling, milestones, conversational assistance, prompt management and Administrator monitoring will also be tested. These functions correspond directly to the capabilities defined for the prototype.
Access-control testing will verify that project information is provided only to authorised users. Test scenarios will confirm that Students can access only their own projects, Mentors can access only their assigned teams, and the Convenor can access all Capstone projects.

Test scenarios will confirm that Students can access only their own projects, Mentors can access only their assigned teams, and the Convenor can access all Capstone projects. Both authorised and unauthorised access attempts will be tested to ensure that project-specific information remains separated between projects.
AI response evaluation will use a predefined set of representative general Capstone questions, project-specific questions and deliberately unanswerable questions. Responses will be assessed for relevance, grounded accuracy, hallucination occurrence, fallback behaviour and latency. Prompt configurations will also be refined iteratively, with selected prompt versions compared using the same representative questions to determine whether changes improve response quality and reduce unsupported outputs. This follows the AI evaluation approach already established for the prototype.
User Acceptance Testing (UAT) will be used to determine whether the prototype is understandable, usable and suitable for its intended Capstone activities. Representative users and project stakeholders will complete defined scenarios and provide feedback on the usefulness of the prototype and its AI-generated responses. Feedback gathered through prototype demonstrations and UAT will be considered when refining the final system.

documents.text: To identify a specific real-world micro-friction and rapidly develop a functional AI-driven prototype using the Agentaus API. The team will apply Agile practices to scope the problem, design and test AI prompts, integrate the API, develop an MVP, and evaluate the solution within the 10-week project timeline.

Table row 1: Role | Name (s) | Responsiblity
Table row 2: Project Manager | Munkhuu Bold | Facilitates Scrum events, supports the team in following Agile practices, removes impediments, and promotes continuous improvement.
Table row 3: Quality & AI Lead | Ashly Shaji | Represents the project requirements, prioritises the product backlog, defines priorities, and ensures the MVP delivers value to the intended users.
Table row 4: Developer / Tech Lead | Prachi Sherkar | Collaboratively analyses the problem, develops the solution, integrates the Agentaus API, designs prompts, tests AI outputs, and builds the MVP.
Table row 5: Developer / Tech Lead | Chernor Bah | Collaboratively analyses the problem, develops the solution, integrates the Agentaus API, designs prompts, tests AI outputs, and builds the MVP.

Values: Commitment, courage, focus, openness, respect, and accountability.
Agreements: Team members will attend scheduled meetings, communicate progress and blockers openly, respect different ideas and perspectives, complete agreed tasks within sprint timeframes, and provide constructive feedback. Decisions will be made collaboratively, with the team remaining focused on the agreed project scope.

Stakeholders: Trellis Data, academic mentor, project team, and the intended users of the selected AI solution.
Interests: Stakeholders are primarily interested in a functional, technically feasible, and user-focused prototype that demonstrates effective use of the Agentaus API and addresses a clearly defined real-world problem.

The project depends on the availability and functionality of the Agentaus API, access to relevant data or information required by the selected use case, and timely feedback from the sponsor and academic mentor. The team also depends on effective coordination between problem analysis, prompt engineering, API integration, front-end development, and evaluation activities.

Criteria: Success will be measured by the team's ability to deliver a functional MVP within the 10-week timeline, successfully integrate the Agentaus API, demonstrate effective prompt engineering, and evaluate the solution against defined criteria for AI accuracy, response quality, latency, usability, and alignment with the identified user problem.

Criteria: A task or sprint deliverable is considered complete when the agreed requirements have been implemented, the functionality has been tested, relevant AI outputs have been evaluated, integration works as intended, identified issues have been addressed or documented, and the work is committed to the project repository with appropriate documentation.

Methodology: Scrum-based Agile development using short, focused sprints within the 10-week project timeline.
Events: Sprint planning, regular team stand-ups/check-ins, sprint reviews, backlog refinement, and sprint retrospectives. Sprint activities will focus on progressive development of the problem definition, AI architecture, API integration, MVP, testing, and evaluation.

Internal: Regular team meetings and stand-ups will be used to coordinate tasks, communicate progress, identify blockers, and manage sprint priorities. Day-to-day communication will be conducted through the team's agreed communication channel.
External: Communication with the project sponsor and academic mentor will occur through scheduled meetings and agreed communication channels, with progress, key decisions, questions, and project risks communicated clearly and in a timely manner.

Risks: Key risks include unclear problem scope, feature creep, AI hallucinations or inaccurate outputs, API limitations or failures, technical integration issues, limited development time, and uneven team availability.
Mitigation: The team will maintain a prioritised backlog, define a clear MVP scope, test and refine prompts, establish evaluation criteria for AI outputs, prototype API integration early, document technical issues, and regularly review project risks during sprint planning and retrospectives.

The team will use sprint retrospectives to regularly review what went well, what could be improved, and what actions should be taken in the next sprint. Feedback from the sponsor, academic mentor, testing, and AI evaluation will also be used to refine the product, development process, and team collaboration throughout the project.
By signing this charter, each team member acknowledges their commitment to the above terms and the success of the project.
